hints: Look at the red blood cell in the drawing (7 mm) and ask yourself, what is the real diameter of a human red blood cell in micrometres?
Use linear magnification = image size divided by actual size, after converting both to the same units (remember $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$).
walkthrough:
**Recall the true size of a red blood cell**

A prepared 9700 student knows a human red blood cell is tiny, about $7 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ in diameter. This is your actual size. The drawing size is your image size, $7 \text{ mm}$.

**Convert to the same units**

You cannot divide mm by micrometres directly, so convert first. Since $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$:
$$7 \text{ mm} = 7 \times 1000 = 7000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$$

**Apply the magnification formula**

Linear magnification tells you how many times bigger the drawing is:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}} = \frac{7000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}}{7 \text{ } \mu\text{m}} = 1000$$
So the drawing is $\times 1000$.

**Check it makes sense with the other cells**

A neutrophil is really about $12$ to $14 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$. At $\times 1000$, $14 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ becomes $14 \text{ mm}$, exactly as drawn. A small lymphocyte is really about $6 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$, which becomes $6 \text{ mm}$. Everything fits.

options.A: Much too small. At x10 a $7 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ red cell would only be $0.07 \text{ mm}$ in the drawing, not $7 \text{ mm}$.
options.B: Still far too small. At x40 a red cell would only be about $0.28 \text{ mm}$ in the drawing.
options.C: Ten times too small. At x100 a $7 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ red cell would be $0.7 \text{ mm}$, not $7 \text{ mm}$.
options.D: Correct. $7000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ divided by $7 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ = 1000, and this also correctly predicts the lymphocyte and neutrophil drawing sizes.
